title: 7 best eesel AI alternatives for ecommerce customer support (2026)
summary: Compare seven eesel AI alternatives by which ecommerce actions each one takes without an agent approving it, from refunds and cancellations to subscriptions.
body_markdown:
## How to choose the right eesel AI alternative


Teams that get further with AI see it in their numbers. Deloitte Digital's 2026 Global Contact Center Survey found that contact centers with mature AI capabilities report[85% greater contact center profitability](https://www.deloittedigital.com/us/en/news/press-releases/2026/deloitte-digital-2026-global-contact-center-survey.html) than low-maturity peers, so choosing a platform that can offer more advanced AI functionality as you're ready for it is key here.


Four things separate these tools in practice. They are how much of the queue you can hand off, how many ecommerce actions each tool can take, how it fits your helpdesk, and what each resolution really costs.


### Check how much of the queue each tool can resolve without approval


Start with the share of tickets you'd let the AI resolve without anyone approving them. If half your queue still runs through drafts, your agents are still reviewing half your queue. Response checks, hard caps on refunds, and handoff rules for each ticket type all raise that share, because they catch problems before a reply goes out.


### Check which ecommerce actions each tool can take


If you're moving off eesel, start by listing the actions eesel doesn't take today. eesel's[Shopify integration](https://docs.eesel.ai/integrations/e-commerce/shopify) can issue refunds, create returns, cancel unfulfilled orders, and update shipping addresses. It can't manage subscriptions or generate return labels, so those tickets still go to your agents.


Action coverage varies widely across the[best AI customer service platforms](https://yuma.ai/blogs/best-ai-customer-service-platforms) . Some tools like Yuma can process a refund in Shopify and change a subscription automatically.


Others cover only part of the job. Some may require handoffs to human agents for order modifications or cancellations, for example.


A tool that explains your refund policy but can't issue the refund still leaves the work with your agents. Before you commit, check each action you need against the vendor's own docs.


### Compare total cost of ownership


Monthly sticker prices don't compare well across the pricing models on this list, so cost per resolved ticket is the more useful number. Add up the tool's cost and the agent time spent reviewing drafts, then divide by the tickets the AI actually closed. Credit-based plans count each ticket the AI works on, while per-resolution plans charge only for tickets the AI fully resolves.


### Check how each tool fits your current helpdesk


The tools here fall into three groups, and each one changes how much of your setup you keep.


- **Tools that work inside your helpdesk:** Yuma, eesel, My AskAI, Fini, and Fin. You keep your helpdesk and change the AI layer.
- **Helpdesks with native AI:** Gorgias, Zendesk, and Freshdesk. The AI comes with the helpdesk, so switching tools can mean switching helpdesks.
- **Standalone AI support platforms:** Tidio, Chatling, and Chatbase. These run their own inbox and channels, with varying helpdesk connections.


If your helpdesk works and the AI is what's missing, a tool that works inside it might be the lowest-friction path. If the helpdesk itself is the problem, a platform switch can make sense. Either way, account for the systems your team already uses today before comparing[AI customer service software](https://yuma.ai/blogs/ai-customer-service-software) .


## How to know a ticket type is ready to run without approval


Draft mode is a reasonable way to start with any AI tool, eesel included. It lets your team see the replies and actions the AI would take before customers do. The risk is that it never ends, and the review queue quietly becomes a permanent part of the job.


To avoid that, treat each ticket type as its own trial. Take address changes, for example. A customer emails about an order of a pair of running shoes, asking to send it to her new apartment before it ships. Here's how that ticket type can move from draft to running without approval.


- **Weeks 1 and 2, every reply is a draft.** The AI drafts the reply and queues the address update. An agent checks that the order hasn't shipped, confirms the new address, and sends. When a draft is wrong, like promising a change on an order that's already with the carrier, the agent fixes it and logs why.
- **Weeks 3 and 4, the team fixes the gaps.** The edit log shows a pattern, such as shipped orders getting the same promise as unshipped ones. The team adds a rule to its help docs or SOPs so shipped orders go to a person.
- **Week 5, the category hits its target.** The team agreed on a target up front, for example 9 in 10 drafts sent unedited for three weeks straight. Address changes clear it, so the team lets the AI update addresses without approval, with shipped orders still routed to a person.
- **After that, spot-checks replace reviews.** An agent reviews a sample of resolved address changes each week instead of every ticket.


How one ticket type moves from draft mode to running without approval.


If a category is ready but your tool can't safely take the next step, with caps on sensitive actions and clear handoff rules, it's time to look at alternatives. And if agents keep editing drafts in every category, the AI is probably missing information or rules. In that case, fix your help docs and SOPs before adding more automation.
